# Headlines — review guidance

Read under [Headlines](headlines.md). Read the text first and say its angle to yourself in one sentence. Then read the headline against that sentence, and each subheading against its own section and against any quotation standing under it, and ask four questions of each. Can every word in it be supported by the text? Is the core message there? Does the tone match the seriousness of the content? Would the reader feel misled afterwards?

## Avoid

Each of these in a headline or a subheading is a finding where you can name what a reader of that heading loses, and no finding where you cannot. A reader loses something where the heading claims more than the text, or something other than it; is louder in tone than the text; says again, in substance, what stands under it; gives away the point of a quotation under it; is a bare label or subject where the text has an angle, or a question where the text answers it; uses words the audience does not know; or leaves a reader who sees only the heading unable to tell what the text is about. Those are instances of the test and not the whole of it, so an item they do not name is still a finding wherever the test holds, as where a colon in place of a verb leaves the reader unable to tell who did what. A loss is something the reader gets wrong or does not get: what the text claims, how seriously it speaks, what it is about, a quotation's point met fresh. A heading that could be clearer, more specific, more complete or closer to the angle you would have chosen loses its reader nothing, and on a finished text it is left as it is:

- Claims, figures, names or conclusions not found in the text. A headline that sharpens, generalises or draws a conclusion the text itself does not draw is always a finding, however well it reads.
- Vague or mysterious wording that requires reading the text to understand the headline.
- A subject named with nothing said about it, where the text has an angle to state.
- Words, names and abbreviations the audience will not know.
- Partial quotes, colons in place of a verb, stilted headline-speak.
- Puns and references that fail for anyone who does not get the allusion.
- Question headlines. Where the text gives the answer, the headline gives it too. The exceptions are a text built as questions and answers, where the form is natural, and a text that truly leaves the question open, where the headline is deliberately kept from asserting anything.
- A tone more dramatic than the text's.
- The same words and phrasing in the headline and the standfirst or opening paragraph, or in a subheading and the first sentence under it. They complement each other; they do not repeat.
- A subheading that pre-spends the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under it, so that the reader meets the quotation as the subheading said again. A label on a reference or navigation text is correct as a label.

- An allusion or an image that still tells a reader who sees only the heading what the text is about. It names the text's subject, and may name it in general terms where the text's first lines give the particulars. One that names no subject at all leaves its reader unable to tell what the text is about, however soon the body resolves it, and that is a finding.

# The anti-slop catalogue

Prose that a language model produced, or that a human wrote after reading a great deal of it, fails in a small number of recognisable ways. This is the catalogue of those ways: what each one looks like on the page, why it costs the reader something, and the smallest change that removes it. It is a diagnostic document — a Skill reading it beside the base contract meets no target the contract does not already hold, and a Skill reading it alone has the patterns and their repairs and needs nothing else.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language, and do not look for the English words in it. A word, a phrase, a punctuation convention, or a construction that only exists in one language belongs to that language's own anti-slop guidance instead, where a Skill loads it beside this file.

## The test before a pattern is recorded

Each pattern below says what a phrase looks like, and looking like one is not being one. Make the repair in your head before you record anything: where the text then asserts more, less or something else than it did, or a distinction it drew is gone, the pattern is not present and nothing is recorded. A hedge that marks genuine doubt, a repetition that lands, a contrast the reader really would otherwise draw wrongly — each of them fails that test, and each is left exactly as it stands.

The test comes before the finding rather than after it. A pattern written down reaches whoever repairs it as a defect somebody found, and a guard that only makes the repair careful arrives too late to save the phrase.

Repair with the smallest change that removes a pattern the test admits. The writer's vocabulary, their bluntness, their humour, their admitted uncertainty, and their rhythm are what makes a text theirs; a pass that tidies all of it into even prose has replaced one machine voice with another. Leave a strong sentence alone even where it is unusual.

## The seven patterns

**False contrasts.** A negation used as a run-up to the actual claim: *This isn't a tool. It's a way of working.* *The question isn't whether, but when.* *It's not just faster — it's cheaper.* The rejected half was never in play, so the sentence spends the reader's attention establishing a position nobody held. State the second half on its own: *This changes how the team works.* A contrast stays where the text really is correcting something a reader would otherwise believe.

**Empty openings.** A first sentence that announces the subject, asserts that the subject matters, or clears the throat before the text starts: *In today's rapidly changing landscape…*, *Communication has never been more important.*, *Here's the thing.*, *What most people get wrong is…* Each could sit in front of any text at all, which is the test: an opening that would survive being moved to a different article is carrying no information. Cut it and open on the material — a fact, a scene, a tension, the question the text answers. The second paragraph is very often the real opening.

**Importance inflation.** Adjectives and formulas that assert weight the material has not shown: *a pivotal moment*, *stands as a testament to*, *a game-changer*, *underscores the significance of*, *plays a vital role in*. Also the trailing participial clause that pretends to interpret — *…, highlighting the team's commitment to quality* — which adds a judgement no fact in the sentence supports. Replace the assertion with what actually happened: *The launch is the company's first paid product.* A reader who is given the fact will decide it matters without being told to.

**Vague attribution.** A claim credited to nobody: *Studies show*, *experts agree*, *industry reports suggest*, *it is widely believed*, *many argue*. Nothing here can be checked, and nothing can be contradicted, which is precisely what makes it comfortable to write. Name who found it, who said it, and how they know; where the text has no source, cut the claim rather than dressing it. Do not invent an attribution to satisfy the pattern — an unsourced sentence is removed, never furnished with a plausible source.

**Synonym cycling.** One thing given a new name every time it is mentioned, because repeating a word felt like poor style: *the agent* reviews the draft, then *the assistant* scores it, then *the tool* suggests fixes. A reader who has been introduced to three names reasonably assumes three things. Pick the clear name and repeat it. Repetition of a key term is how a reader knows it is the same term, and the fix is usually one word restored in two places rather than a rewritten paragraph. The pattern is present only where the names denote one thing: two words a text uses for two things are not cycling however often they alternate, and a text that named two things comes back naming two things.

**Robotic rhythm.** Sentences and paragraphs built to one template: the same length, the same shape, the same three-part list, each paragraph opening with its topic sentence and closing with its summary. Stacked short fragments used for drama — *That's it. That's the whole idea.* — are the same fault at the other extreme. Read a passage aloud in your head; where the breath falls in the same place every time, the shape is doing the writing. Vary length and construction where the meaning gives you a reason to, and merge or split only the sentences whose shape is actually the problem.

**Generic conclusions.** A final paragraph that restates what the reader has just read, reopens the introduction as a rhetorical question, or reaches for an uplifting abstraction: *In conclusion*, *Ultimately, the future belongs to those who…*, *one thing is clear.* The reader was there for the whole text and does not need it summarised back. Delete the paragraph and end on the last concrete point the draft already contains; where the job genuinely calls for a conclusion, a recommendation, or a next step, write that thing plainly and stop. Do not replace a weak closing metaphor with a better one — remove it.

# The correction brief

Give this to a subagent started fresh for one correction, filled in from the run as it now stands. Everything in angle brackets is replaced; nothing else is rewritten.

`<text>` is the current Text Artifact pasted whole — the text as it stands after every correction so far, never the text as it arrived and never an extract of it. `<findings>` is every finding of the most recent review, in the order it was recorded, each pasted whole under the same rule. `<genre>`, `<technique>` and `<language>` are the values the run resolved, written as the resources are named; write `none` for `<technique>` where no technique was resolved, and drop the sentence naming its resource with it. `<library>` is the Collection Library path this run resolved.

A brief-shortfall finding also carries its numbered requirement and exact, attributed supporting passages supplied by the parent review. Those are part of the finding, not an extra interpretation.

Tell the subagent nothing else. Not what an earlier round found, not what an earlier correction attempted, not which findings you think matter most, and not your reading of what the text is trying to do — that reading is the thing a fresh subagent is dispatched to be without.

Hand the filled-in brief to the subagent directly, as the whole of its instruction, and hand it over no other way. Never write it to a file and send a path in its place: this brief holds the user's text entire and every finding standing against it, and a file is a name some other process can read, replace, or delete for as long as the round lasts. A long text makes a long brief, and a long brief is passed whole anyway — trimming it, summarising it, and pointing at it are the three things this brief exists to rule out.

---

You are making one correction to one text. You have not seen this text before, and there is nothing you are expected to remember: the text below is its current state, and the findings below are the current review's, complete and as they were written. Repair them.

**The text.** This is the complete Text Artifact, exactly as it now stands:

`<text>`

**The findings.** This is every finding the review recorded against that text, complete and in the order it recorded them:

`<findings>`

You are making one correction to one text. You have not seen this text before, and there is nothing you are expected to remember: the text below is its current state, and the findings below are the current review's, complete and as they were written. Repair them.

**The text.** This is the complete Text Artifact, exactly as it now stands:

````markdown
# Tallmora Energi inviger den 3 juni en ny solpark med 12 000 solpaneler vid Kvarnbacken i Tallmora

Tallmora Energi AB inviger den 3 juni 2027 en ny solpark vid Kvarnbacken i Tallmora, på den mark där kommunens grustäkt låg fram till 2019. Parken har 12 000 solpaneler på 18 hektar, har kostat 64 miljoner kronor att bygga och beräknas ge 7,5 gigawattimmar el om året, vilket enligt bolagets egen beräkning motsvarar hushållselen i omkring 1 500 villor i kommunen.

”Solparken visar att en gammal grustäkt kan göra nytta igen. Vi tror att fler kommuner kommer att pröva samma lösning”, säger Maria Ekholm, vd för Tallmora Energi.

”Vi vill att elen som används i Tallmora också ska produceras här. Parken har kostat 64 miljoner kronor och ger 7,5 gigawattimmar om året”, säger Johan Berg, styrelseordförande i Tallmora Energi.

Siffran för årsproduktionen är en uppskattning, och den verkliga produktionen beror på hur soligt året blir.

Elen levereras till elnätet och säljs inte direkt till hushållen i närheten.

Området är inhägnat och inte öppet för allmänheten, utom vid invigningen den 3 juni klockan 14.00–16.00, då bolaget visar parken för besökare.

Grustäkten vid Kvarnbacken avvecklades 2019. Tallmora Energi fick tillstånd att bygga solparken 2025, och bygget började i augusti 2026.

Noter till redaktionen: Parken har 40 växelriktare. Panelerna står i rader i öst–västlig riktning, och markytan mellan raderna betas av får från en gård i närheten. Bilder från solparken finns på https://example.se/press/kvarnbacken-bilder.

Kontakt: Lina Sjögren, kommunikationschef, Tallmora Energi, 070-000 00 00, lina.sjogren@example.se

Tallmora Energi AB ägs av Tallmora kommun och levererar el och fjärrvärme till omkring 14 000 kunder i kommunen.
````

(The text is everything between the four-backtick fence lines; the fence is not part of it. The file ends with a single newline after the last line.)

**The findings.** This is every finding the review recorded against that text, complete and in the order it recorded them:

1. **Rubriken är över gränsen.** Rubriken (”Tallmora Energi inviger den 3 juni en ny solpark med 12 000 solpaneler vid Kvarnbacken i Tallmora”) är 97 tecken inklusive mellanslag enligt mätskriptet; genren tillåter högst 70. Krav: pressreleasegenren, ”The headline states the news on one line … at most 70 characters”. Vad läsaren förlorar: en redaktör som ser rubriken i en lista eller ett nyhetsflöde får den avkortad, och rubriken bär detaljer (antal paneler, ortnamnet två gånger) som ingressen redan har i sin helhet.

2. **Ingressen är över gränsen.** Ingressen, första stycket efter rubriken, är 62 ord enligt mätskriptet; genren tillåter högst 60. Krav: ”The summary is at most 60 words.” Vad läsaren förlorar: den notis en journalist ska kunna kopiera rakt av är längre än genren lovar. Enligt granskningsanvisningen flyttas det som inte behövs för notisen helt till brödtexten i stället för att strykas.

3. **Ingressens första mening upprepar rubrikens formulering.** Ingressen öppnar ”Tallmora Energi AB inviger den 3 juni 2027 en ny solpark vid Kvarnbacken i Tallmora”, som är rubrikens mening i rubrikens ordning med bara ”AB” och årtalet tillagda. Krav: pressreleasegenren – ingressen återger rubrikens nyhet i sin helhet men med egna ord, och är aldrig rubrikens formulering sagd igen; rubriken och det som följer säger olika saker med olika ord (headlines.md). Vad läsaren förlorar: redaktören läser samma mening två gånger i de enda två meningar hen säkert läser. (Delade namn, siffror och ordet för det som tillkännages är ingen upprepning; det är ordföljden och formuleringen som upprepas.)

4. **De två citaten står direkt efter varandra, utan brödtext emellan.** Johan Bergs citat står omedelbart efter Maria Ekholms, och brödtexten kommer först efter båda. Krav: pressreleasegenren – det första citatet står direkt efter ingressen, det andra efter brödtexten. # Press release

An announcement written for the editor deciding whether there is a story here and for the journalist who may take facts from it and publish them. It is not written for the public: it is written for the person standing between an organisation and the public, and it works when they can do their job from it without ringing to ask what something meant.

Write the headline as [Headlines](../headlines.md) says, within the limit below.

## What this genre asks for

**A recipient meets the parts in the order they expect them.** An editor works through many releases in a day and reads each one by habit, finding the next thing where the last release had it, so a release that rearranges the parts spends that habit before its facts get a hearing. A headline and a summary come first and work as a news item together, so that a recipient who reads no further has still been told the news. A short quotation follows the summary, saying what somebody makes of the news. The body comes next and can be facts alone, because the comment has already been made, and a second quotation after it carries one of the most important messages the sender wants the recipient to take away. Then comes what serves the recipient rather than the story: background they may use or leave, the links and attachments that go with the release, the contact details, and last of all a standing description of the organisation. A release owes no heading announcing each part: a recipient finds each one by where it stands.

**The headline states the news on one line.** The headline is the release's level-1 heading (`h1` in HTML, `#` in Markdown). The headline is at most 70 characters, spaces included. It interests an editor by the news it states and never by a word louder than that news: a figure that carries the news belongs in it, and a word of praise, excitement or urgency does not. A time from which the release may be published, where the material states one, stands on a line of its own above the headline, never between the headline and the summary.

**The summary tells the news in full.** The summary is the first paragraph after the headline. The summary is at most 60 words. It names the organisation sending the release and says what has happened or will happen, so that a journalist can copy the headline and the summary into a news item and publish it. A dateline, where the release carries one, opens that paragraph rather than standing as a paragraph of its own. The summary restates the headline's news in full, in its own words, and adds the sender and the particulars: a reader who has just read the headline meets the same news told fully, and never the headline's wording said again. The rule in [Headlines](../headlines.md) that a headline and what follows say different things in different words therefore holds here for the words and the detail and not for the news, since the two together are the notice.

**The news is in the first sentence.** The summary opens with what has happened or will happen, who is doing it, and when. That sentence and the headline above it are the only ones an editor is certain to read, and an opening that describes the organisation, sets a scene, or announces that an announcement is being made has spent them on nothing.

**Every fact is in a form that can be printed.** Dates in full, times and opening hours as they will appear, amounts with their currency and the period they cover, counts as counts, names with the roles that make them relevant, and places spelled as the recipient spells them. A recipient should be able to lift any fact straight into their own text and be right.

**What the announcement excludes is said.** Where a reader would reasonably assume something the material rules out — that a service does a thing it does not do, that a figure covers more than it covers, that a trial is a permanent arrangement — the release says so plainly and once. A sentence costs less than the correction it prevents.

**A quotation is a person saying something only they could say.** Where the material carries an attributed quotation, it appears with the speaker's name and the role that entitles them to what they are saying. Where the material carries none, none is written; a manufactured sentence of enthusiasm is the first thing an editor deletes and the first sign that the rest may be padded too. A quotation carries what somebody makes of the news — an interpretation, a conclusion, a view, a message — and never a fact or a figure of its own: a fact the news depends on stands in the summary or the body, where a journalist can lift it without the quotation marks.

**Each quotation has its place.** The first stands directly after the summary: it is short, comments on the news, draws a conclusion from it and takes a view. The second stands after the body and carries one of the most important messages the sender wants a recipient to take away, and no new fact or figure. Where the material carries one quotation, the release carries that one, directly after the summary, and it carries the message where the material gives it one. Where the material carries two and neither carries a message, each stands in its place as the material gives it, and no message is written into either. Where the material carries none, the release has no quotation, and the gap is the material's: said, never filled.

**The body is one or two short paragraphs.** They complement and deepen the summary, and they are neutral enough that a journalist can lift them straight into their own text without rewriting the substance.

**It reads as information rather than as selling.** The recipient's job is to be sceptical of it, and prose that argues for its subject invites exactly the scepticism the facts then have to survive. What survives is what the material supports and the recipient can check.

**What the release ends with is the material's.** The background carries what a journalist may use and may just as well leave out, so nothing the news depends on is left to it. Nothing stands below the release as notes to the editor: detail a journalist may use is background, and a link or an attachment stands with the links and attachments. The links and attachments are what accompanies the release — images, pages on the web, documents — named or linked, and nothing written about them. The contact is a named person a journalist can turn to with further questions: their name, their title, a telephone number and an email address, as far as the material gives them; a name by itself is not a contact. The standing description is a short, factual and neutrally worded account of what the organisation does, written for a journalist's use, and it stops there. Where the material gives nothing for one of these parts, or gives only some of a contact's details, the release goes without what is missing rather than with something written to fill the place.

**It is short.** A release is a page and not a document. Detail beyond what the news needs goes into the background or is left for the recipient to ask about.

## What this genre does not do

It does not write the journalist's article for them, and it does not narrate. Background, colour, and interpretation are theirs to add or leave out; what the release owes them is the news, the facts in a usable form, and somebody to ask.

It adds no requirement the base contract already holds. Register, structure, sentences, words, claims, openings, endings, formatting, and consistency are stated there once, and a rule repeated here would be one rule made into two things to keep true.

## The technique this genre is ordinarily written with

None. The order of the parts above is the whole of a release's structure, and it is a recipient's habit rather than an arc: the news, what somebody makes of it, the facts to lift, and the message the sender stands behind. An arc built over it would take the news off the first sentence, which is the one thing a release cannot spend.
# Press release — review guidance

Diagnostics for the requirements the press release genre's base half states, for a Skill reviewing a draft written against them. Nothing here is a requirement: every target a draft has to meet is in the base half, where the Skill that wrote the draft could see it, and a finding raised here is raised against a rule stated there. The examples are English and are patterns — apply what one does, in the language of the draft, rather than looking for its words.

## The shape

**Test.** Read the draft for its parts alone, ignoring how well each one is written, and check the sequence against the one the base half states — headline, summary, the first quotation, the body, the second quotation, the background, the links and attachments, the contact and the standing description. A part standing somewhere else in that sequence is a finding, and so is a part the material supplies and the draft leaves out. A block of notes to the editor, wherever it stands and whatever it is labelled, is a part outside the sequence and a finding of its own: the base half has no place for it, so its detail belongs in the background and its links with the links and attachments. Reading such a block as the background, because it holds background, leaves the recipient a part they do not expect.

**Failure.** A paragraph about what the organisation does before the news; the standing description at the top, or worked into the body as though it were background; contact details between body paragraphs; a comment placed before the recipient has been told what it is a comment on; the only comment standing between body paragraphs; background spliced through the body, so a journalist cannot lift a passage without carrying it along; detail kept below the release as notes where the background is its place; a publication time between the headline and the summary.

**Edge.** A part the material cannot supply is absent rather than invented, and that is a finding against the material rather than against the order: a release with one quotation or none is a whole release, and a release with no links, no attachments or no background is too. The parts are what a recipient expects to find and not sections to be labelled: a release carrying them in order owes no heading announcing each one, and a part is not missing because it runs to a single paragraph. A publication time on its own line above the headline is where the base half puts it, and no part out of order.

**Minimum safe correction.** Move the misplaced part whole and change nothing inside it — a part in the wrong place is rarely also badly written, and rewriting it while moving it turns one finding into two. Where a part is missing and the material carries what it needs, assemble it from the material. Where the material carries nothing for it, leave it out and raise the finding against the material. Fold a block of notes to the editor into the background whole, after whatever background there is, move its links to the links and attachments, and drop the label it carried; change nothing inside the detail it moves. Never write a quotation the material does not have to fill a place in the sequence.

## The headline

**Test.** Count the headline's characters, spaces included, before reporting its length against the limit the base half states, and give the count. Then read the headline alone and ask whether it states the news on one line — what has happened or will happen — so that an editor who reads nothing else knows what the release announces.

**Failure.** A headline over the limit; a headline naming the organisation or the subject and nothing that happened; two news items joined into one headline; a headline that promises interest with a word — *exciting*, *major*, *big news* — where it should state what makes the news.

**Edge.** Whether it has an active verb, the present tense and a figure is what the headline guidance diagnoses, not this section. A plain headline stating the news is working; plain is no defect, and a headline with no figure where no figure carries the news is working too.

**Minimum safe correction.** Rewrite the headline alone, from the news the summary states and at its strength, and measure it again. Shorten by dropping what the summary already carries in detail, never by dropping the news; never make it louder to make it interesting.

## The summary

**Test.** The summary is the first paragraph after the headline. Count its words before reporting its length against the limit the base half states, and give the count. Then read that paragraph for the sender organisation's name and for the news, told in full enough that the headline and this paragraph would stand together as a news item.

**Failure.** A summary over the limit; a summary that never names the sender; a summary that opens on the organisation's history and reaches the news in its last sentence; a dateline standing as a paragraph of its own, so the paragraph after the headline is not the summary.

**Edge.** A dateline that opens the summary belongs to it and is counted with it. A summary exactly at the limit is inside it.

**Minimum safe correction.** Keep the news, the sender and the particulars a notice needs, and move the rest whole into the body, where a journalist still finds it. Move rather than delete: a fact cut from the summary to meet the limit is a fact the release no longer carries. Measure again after the move.

## The headline and the summary

**Test.** Read the summary against the headline above it. The base half asks the summary to restate the headline's news in full, in its own words, adding the sender and the particulars; read whether it does that, or whether it says the headline again in the headline's own wording.

**Failure.** A summary whose first sentence is the headline's sentence with a date added; a summary built from the headline's own phrases in the headline's own order.

**Edge.** A summary restating the headline's news in its own words, and adding the sender and the particulars, is the notice this genre asks for and no finding under the headline guidance's item on a heading that says again, in substance, what stands under it — the news is meant to stand in both. Shared names, figures and the one word for the thing announced are not the headline's wording said again; a summary that repeats the headline's wording is still a finding.

**Minimum safe correction.** Reword the summary's opening sentence in its own words at the same strength, keeping every fact and figure it carries, and measure the summary again.

## The first sentence

**Test.** Read the summary's first sentence alone and ask whether an editor could tell from it what happened, who did it, and when. Anything they would have to read on to learn is a finding.

**Failure.** *Fagervik City Library is delighted to announce a new initiative* — an announcement about an announcement. *For many households, a broken appliance means an expensive choice* — a scene that could open anything. A first sentence naming the organisation and its values before it names the news.

**Edge.** Where the material genuinely has no date — a thing that has already happened and is being announced now — the *when* is that it has happened, and the sentence says so rather than manufacturing a schedule.

**Minimum safe correction.** Find the sentence in the draft that does carry the news, move it to the front of the summary, and delete the opening it replaces. Where no sentence carries it, assemble one from the material's own facts and nothing else.

## Printable facts

**Test.** Take each fact in the draft and ask whether it could be typed straight into somebody else's article. A fact that would prompt a phone call is a finding.

**Failure.** *This spring* where the material gives a date; *evenings* where it gives opening hours; *substantial municipal funding* where it gives an amount; a name without the role that makes the person relevant; an amount without its currency or its period.

**Edge.** A fact the material itself leaves vague stays vague in the release and is not sharpened. Precision that the material does not carry is invention, whatever it does for the release.

**Minimum safe correction.** Replace the vague form with the material's own value. Where the material has no value, leave the vague form and raise the finding against the material rather than filling it in.

## Exclusions

**Test.** Read the draft as a busy journalist would and note what you now believe. Check each belief against the material, especially the ones the material explicitly rules out.

**Failure.** A release about a repair workshop that never says visitors repair their own devices, leaving a reader to write that the library repairs them; a trial year presented without the word that makes it a trial; a service described in terms that imply parts are sold.

**Edge.** A release does not list everything it is not. The exclusion belongs in the release where a reader would otherwise assume the opposite, and nowhere else.

**Minimum safe correction.** Add one plain sentence carrying the material's own exclusion, placed where the misreading would occur. Do not restructure the release around it.

## Quotations

**Test.** For each quotation, ask whether the named person is the only sort of person who could have said it, and whether the material carries it.

**Failure.** *We are excited to offer this service to our community, said the library director* — attributable to anybody, informative to nobody. A quotation assembled from a paraphrase in the material. A quotation carrying a fact that appears nowhere else and nowhere in the source.

**Edge.** A quotation may be shortened or its spoken syntax repaired within the boundary the writing Skill works under; what a review finds here is a quotation the material does not support at all, or one that says nothing.

**Minimum safe correction.** Replace it with what the material has the person saying, or remove the quotation. Removing it is always safe; writing a better one is not.

## Where the quotations stand

**Test.** Find each quotation and name the part on either side of it. With two, the first stands directly after the summary and the second after the body. With one, it stands directly after the summary. With none, there is nothing to place.

**Failure.** Both quotations after the body, so the news reaches the body with nobody having said what it means; the only quotation after the body or at the end; the first quotation between two body paragraphs; a quotation standing inside the summary, so the notice a journalist copies carries it; the two quotations standing side by side, with no body between them.

**Edge.** A release with one quotation, or none, because the material carries one or none, is placed correctly and owes nothing further; the gap is the material's, and a review writes no quotation into it. Where the material carries two and neither carries a message, each is placed as the base half says and neither is rewritten to carry one.

**Minimum safe correction.** Move the quotation whole, with its attribution, to its place, and change nothing inside it. Never write a quotation the material does not have, and never split one quotation into two to fill both places.

## The second quotation

**Test.** Read the second quotation for what it carries. It is there for one of the sender's most important messages; mark every fact and figure in it and check whether the release states each one outside the quotation.

**Failure.** *"We will have 180,000 kronor for the year and five volunteers on Tuesdays and Thursdays," says the head librarian* — the body's facts put in a speaker's mouth; a second quotation carrying the only mention of an amount, a date or a count; a second quotation repeating the first one's comment on the news with no message of its own.

**Edge.** A figure the quotation uses to make its message, and which the release states outside it, is part of the message rather than a new fact. A second quotation that the material gives without a message stays as the material gives it, and that is a finding against the material rather than a place to write one.

**Minimum safe correction.** Where the material carries the fact outside the quotation, state it in the body and shorten the quotation to what the speaker says beyond it, within the boundary a quotation may be shortened. Where the material carries the fact only in the speaker's words, leave the quotation as it stands and raise the finding against the material. Never add a message the material does not carry.

## The body's length

**Test.** Count the body's paragraphs between the first quotation, or the summary where there is none, and the second quotation, or the background where there is none. More than two is a finding, and so are two paragraphs long enough that a journalist cannot lift either as a passage.

**Failure.** Three or four body paragraphs working through every detail the material holds; a body carrying the organisation's history, which is background; a body that repeats the summary before it deepens it.

**Edge.** A single paragraph is a body. A body that is short because the material is short owes no second paragraph.

**Minimum safe correction.** Keep the paragraphs that complement and deepen the summary, and move the rest whole into the background. Move rather than delete: a fact moved is a fact a journalist can still use.

## Information rather than selling

**Test.** Mark every adjective and adverb of praise, novelty, or scale, then check each against the material.

**Failure.** *Unique*, *revolutionary*, *market-leading*, *long-awaited*, and *proud to* where the material establishes none of them; a benefit asserted for visitors that the material never claims.

**Edge.** A superlative the material states and supports — the first of its kind in the region, where the material says so — stays, with whatever qualification the material gives it.

**Minimum safe correction.** Delete the unsupported modifier and leave the noun. Deletion changes no fact, where rewriting the sentence around the claim often does.

## The close

**Test.** Read the end and ask what a recipient does next. Background they may use, the links and attachments, a contact with a name, a title, a telephone number and an email address as far as the material gives them, and a short standing description where there is one; and above the headline, a publication time where the material states one.

**Failure.** A contact name with no way to reach them; a contact's telephone number or email address in the material and absent from the release; an embargo stated in the material and absent from the release; links to images described in prose instead of given; three paragraphs of organisational history at the end of a page-long release.

**Edge.** A missing contact, or a contact detail the material does not give, is a finding against the material, reported rather than filled, and the same holds for an embargo the material never states.

**Minimum safe correction.** Restore the material's contact details or embargo verbatim, the embargo above the headline, and cut the standing description back at the point it stops being of use to a recipient.

## Length

**Test.** Count. A release running past a page is a finding, whatever else is right about it.

**Failure.** Background the news does not need; the organisation's history; an explanation of why the subject matters in general.

**Edge.** Where a stated length exists, that is the measure. Where none is stated, a page is the shape.

**Minimum safe correction.** Move the surplus into the background, or cut it. Facts are moved rather than deleted where a journalist might want them.

# The base contract

Write with the clarity and factual precision of a well-edited newspaper or quality magazine. Genre, audience, and purpose override that register: a letter, a speech and an advertisement keep their own character. The selected genre governs craft and form; the resolved language governs idiom, syntax and typography. Examples here illustrate meanings, not English phrases to translate.

## Reader and progression

Give the intended reader what they need to understand, judge or do the thing the text is for. Keep a clear focus, introduce unfamiliar concepts before the reasoning needs them, and order material by that reader's needs rather than the writer's discovery process. Relevant technical detail belongs; unexplained jargon and unrelated background do not.

Make the relations between passages real. A transition may explain a connection, but cannot invent one. Keep paragraphs coherent and give supporting material a clear place beside what it supports. The body and its sections remain intelligible without treating a title, standfirst or subheading as their opening sentence.

Open on something specific to the subject. End with what the job calls for: an earned understanding, conclusion, recommendation or next step. Remove introductions and conclusions that add only an announcement or a generic flourish.

## Expression

Use concrete words, useful verbs and a natural, varied cadence. Keep terminology and reference clear; introduce an unfamiliar abbreviation before using it alone. Choose ordinary words where they suffice and established specialist terms where they give this reader precision.

Let tone and rhetorical devices serve the genre and the meaning. A useful analogy, question, image, fragment or humorous turn can clarify or carry a voice; decoration and manufactured drama cannot. An imagined comparison is recognisable as a comparison, never presented as an event or someone's experience. Criticism addresses the supported issue without inventing motives or patronising the reader.

Each passage earns its place. Repetition may establish an independent entry point, explain a hard idea or give a deliberate rhetorical return; merely saying the same thing again does none of these. Keep formatting useful: headings for orientation, lists for coordinate items, tables for comparisons, emphasis for what merits it. Hold voice, terminology and presentation consistent unless a visible purpose calls for a change.

## Claims

Every claim is supported by the text or its material, with exact attribution and proportionate strength. Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened. Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted. A fact, quotation, source, scene, personal experience or opinion attributed to somebody is never invented to complete a form. Name the actual source of an attributed claim rather than invoking unnamed studies or experts.

Circumstantial detail is a claim too: duration, manner, motive, absence and background all need support. So does an evaluative characterisation: calling a count high, low or modest needs a comparison, target, capacity or speaker assessment. Otherwise give the count with its exclusions, without that assessment.

A sequence or correlation establishes no cause. A causal verb such as *shortened* needs causal support; a causal hedge such as *suggests that it shortened* still adds that attribution. This boundary holds in the title, summary, headings and body alike. Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears.

A stated length constrains the use of material and is never a licence to add to it. When the material is insufficient, deliver the length the material supports and name what further material would close the gap. A supplied publication limit is binding; meeting it cannot justify invention or loss of a qualification that changes a claim.
# Reviewing the base contract

Diagnose failures of [the base contract](base.md) in the text in front of you. A finding identifies the passage, the requirement and what the reader loses. Another successful choice, a house-style preference and a mechanical error are not editorial findings; mechanics belongs to the separate final pass. Repetition of whole sentences or passages is an editorial matter, even when the duplication is verbatim; Proofread's duplicate-word correction does not own it.

Read for the intended reader's missing step: an unexplained term, a transition asserting a relation the surrounding sentences do not establish, a section whose place obscures the argument. Cover the paratext to find unresolved references in the body. A heading may carry a fact that the section under it does not repeat: a time, a price or a condition a subheading states has been stated to the reader, and is not missing from the body. What is a finding is a body that needs the heading to be understood — a pronoun, a definite form or an ellipsis that only the heading completes — repaired by naming the referent where the body first needs it rather than by saying the heading's facts again. Judge rhythm by its effect, not sentence counts; purposeful repetition, a personal rough edge and a useful digression may be doing essential work.

Compare the strength of a claim with the support visible in this text. A number contradicting its stated denominator, a causal conclusion following only a sequence, or a certainty contradicted by a nearby qualification is diagnosable. A plausible quotation or experience is not disproved by the absence of its original source. Review no unseen material, request none, and add no source-verification caveat.

Use [the anti-slop catalogue](anti-slop.md) to recognise empty performance, not to prohibit a working figure, contrast or ending. Test suspected filler by what its removal costs; preserve any fact, implication or voice it carries beside the defect. Strong supported criticism needs no generic softening.

A sentence can do its work by bounding what the text asserts: that something is not measured, not claimed, not witnessed or not general, or that what follows is an observation of a document rather than a scene from an occasion. Such a sentence is where *Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened*, *Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted* and *Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears* are carried, and the text alone shows which sentence it is: read it out, and the claims around it assert more than they did. That cost is what the removal test above answers, so recognise one by what it bounds and by which claim loses that bound, never by its form. A finding lies inside such a sentence or nowhere: name a limit another sentence already states in full, or a limit contradicting another passage of this text, or leave the sentence exactly as it stands. Naming the whole of it as the defect names nothing inside it.

Make the smallest correction that removes a finding. Move or clarify existing material where it supplies the missing connection. Introduce no new evidence, experience, attribution or outcome. If repair would change a claim or a quotation's meaning, or requires information absent from the text, leave the passage and report the unresolved finding. A claim removed because the finding named that claim itself remains part of the claim account, and so does every claim a correction left standing with its scope, certainty, attribution, chronology, causality or meaning moved, and every claim a correction added — one the corrected text asserts and the text before it has no counterpart for, an inference drawn from what that text already said among them where it asserts something that text did not say. A claim that has a counterpart in the text before is changed rather than added. A headline, a standfirst and a subheading carry claims like any other passage, and a changed claim is accounted for by what it now asserts rather than how far its wording moved; a correction that took a limit, a connective or a bounding clause out of the text is accounted for by what the reader no longer has, however little of the text went with it. The account is of the text delivered rather than of the text received, and nothing a reviewing Skill says about the claims as a whole contradicts a finding the same reply states.

Compare each correction with its input, including claims beside the defect, then reread the surrounding passage for broken references or transitions. Compare it difference by difference and not by its claims alone, and trace each one to a finding or to what repairing that finding required: a difference answering neither is not a correction, whatever it improves, and the passage it touched belongs back as it was. A correction is a candidate until that comparison and the review after it have run: where the review establishes a defect the correction introduced and its input did not have, the correction is not accepted and its input stands. Preserve functioning wording, voice and formatting outside the finding; concision is not permission to summarise the text away.
# Headlines

How a headline is written, in any genre that links this file. A headline lets the reader judge at once whether the text is for them: it states the core of the text as briefly and precisely as it can, and it is understood on its own, with no image, standfirst or surrounding page to explain it. *Headline* here covers a text's subheadings too; for a subheading, the text is its section.

## Statement or label

A text that reports, explains, argues, decides or narrates gets a statement headline: a clause that says what the text says. A text the reader looks things up in or navigates by — a policy, a manual, opening hours, a contact page — gets a plain label naming what it holds: *Privacy policy*, where a statement would read *How we protect your data*. Everything below is about the statement headline.

## What a statement headline does

- It states the angle: the single most important message, the sentence that would remain if only one could. A subject alone is a label. Test: the headline could not head a different text on the same subject.
- It is a simple clause — subject, active verb, object where there is one — in straight word order, and in the present tense where that fits: *Council introduces free bus travel*.
- The most important keyword comes first.
- A concrete detail stands in it when the detail carries the message: a number, a date, a place. *Three schools to close this autumn* beats *Changes to school organisation*.
- The reader sees what they gain: a decision, a fact, a change. An instructional text may address the reader directly (*you*, *your*) and open on *How to*, *Why* or *Here's*.
- It is as short as the angle allows. Modifiers, repetition and filler go; a keyword that carries meaning stays. The format the text follows sets the limits.
- It sounds like something a person would say aloud.
- Its words are ones this audience knows. A technical term is the right keyword for specialists and noise for a general reader, and the same holds for names and abbreviations.
- Its tone is the text's tone, and never louder. Illness, accidents, crime and crises get a sober, understated headline; a light text can carry more personality.
- It is plain before it is clever. It works in full for a reader who misses every allusion, so a pun or a reference never carries the meaning.
- It gives the answer. Journalists hold a question headline to be the wrong form, and so does this: it is a deliberate exception, natural over a text built as questions and answers, and available where the text truly leaves the question open and the headline is meant to assert nothing.
- The verb does the work. A colon standing in for a verb, a clipped quotation and headline-speak all give way to the full clause.
- It complements what follows. Headline and standfirst, or subheading and the first sentence under it, say different things in different words.

## Every word supported

A headline claims only what its text claims. Every figure, name, claim and conclusion in it is in the text, at the text's own strength: never sharper, never more general, never a conclusion the text does not draw. A reader who finishes the text finds that the headline told the truth about it.

## A subheading over a quotation

A quotation in a section is there to carry what only its speaker can say: a judgement, a figure, a concession. A subheading standing over it, however far down the section the quotation stands, leaves that to the quotation. It states the section's angle from what the rest of the section says, or, where the quotation is the section's point, names the subject, the occasion or the speaker the quotation speaks to, and not the point itself. Test: a reader who has just read the subheading meets the quotation as new material, never as the subheading said again. *The clinic would double its training time*, over a head nurse saying *Next time I would double the training time before we switch*, has spent the quotation before the reader reaches it; *The head nurse looks back on the switch* leaves it to her.

The quotation bridge is the narrative sentence or clause that stands immediately before a quotation and leads the reader into it, including a speech tag that carries anything besides the attribution. The genre that quotes says what a quotation bridge may carry. A subheading standing over a quotation is outside the quotation bridge and is governed by this section.

## Getting there

Settle the reader and the angle before wording anything. Then write three to five variants and keep the clearest, which is rarely the cleverest. Word a subheading from its whole section, once the section is written, in words its first sentence does not use, and leave a quotation standing under it the judgement, figure or concession it is there to carry.
# Headlines — review guidance

Read under [Headlines](headlines.md). Read the text first and say its angle to yourself in one sentence. Then read the headline against that sentence, and each subheading against its own section and against any quotation standing under it, and ask four questions of each. Can every word in it be supported by the text? Is the core message there? Does the tone match the seriousness of the content? Would the reader feel misled afterwards?

## Avoid

Each of these in a headline or a subheading is a finding where you can name what a reader of that heading loses, and no finding where you cannot. A reader loses something where the heading claims more than the text, or something other than it; is louder in tone than the text; says again, in substance, what stands under it; gives away the point of a quotation under it; is a bare label or subject where the text has an angle, or a question where the text answers it; uses words the audience does not know; or leaves a reader who sees only the heading unable to tell what the text is about. Those are instances of the test and not the whole of it, so an item they do not name is still a finding wherever the test holds, as where a colon in place of a verb leaves the reader unable to tell who did what. A loss is something the reader gets wrong or does not get: what the text claims, how seriously it speaks, what it is about, a quotation's point met fresh. A heading that could be clearer, more specific, more complete or closer to the angle you would have chosen loses its reader nothing, and on a finished text it is left as it is:

- Claims, figures, names or conclusions not found in the text. A headline that sharpens, generalises or draws a conclusion the text itself does not draw is always a finding, however well it reads.
- Vague or mysterious wording that requires reading the text to understand the headline.
- A subject named with nothing said about it, where the text has an angle to state.
- Words, names and abbreviations the audience will not know.
- Partial quotes, colons in place of a verb, stilted headline-speak.
- Puns and references that fail for anyone who does not get the allusion.
- Question headlines. Where the text gives the answer, the headline gives it too. The exceptions are a text built as questions and answers, where the form is natural, and a text that truly leaves the question open, where the headline is deliberately kept from asserting anything.
- A tone more dramatic than the text's.
- The same words and phrasing in the headline and the standfirst or opening paragraph, or in a subheading and the first sentence under it. They complement each other; they do not repeat.
- A subheading that pre-spends the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under it, so that the reader meets the quotation as the subheading said again. Read it against the quotation however far down the section the quotation stands. Repair it by naming the subject, the occasion or the speaker, or by stating what the rest of the section says, and leave the quotation as it is.

Name what the reader loses, and repair by rewriting the headline alone, from the text's angle and at the text's own strength. The text stays as it is. A headline or a subheading a round changed is reported with this finding — the part, and the defect that licensed the change — and, where the new one asserts something the old did not, with what it now asserts, so that a reader of the account can tell a repaired part from a rewritten one. A repair keeps the text's recurring words and figures and its meaning: a word or an image the text returns to comes back in the form the text gives it, and the heading names the text's point in the text's own word for it, never in a neighbouring word that widens or shifts what the text says.

## Leave alone

A working headline is left alone. Plain is no defect, and neither is a headline with no number or place where none carries the message, direct address in an instructional text, or an angle other than the one you would have chosen where the text supports it. A label on a reference or navigation text is correct as a label.

Read a heading as its reader meets it, and count a loss that reader would suffer, not one that the strictest reading of a single word could construct. A reader who sees only the heading, as a headline in a list or a search result, has nothing else, so a headline alone has to tell that reader what the text is about. A subheading is met after the headline and the standfirst, so a word or a name they have introduced is known to its reader, and a subheading that refers back to one is not unclear. Four kinds of heading are working, and no *Avoid* item makes one a finding by its wording alone. None of the four overrides the first *Avoid* item, a claim the text does not support as a reader would take it, or the item on a subheading that pre-spends a quotation standing under it:

- An allusion or an image that still tells a reader who sees only the heading what the text is about. It names the text's subject, and may name it in general terms where the text's first lines give the particulars. One that names no subject at all leaves its reader unable to tell what the text is about, however soon the body resolves it, and that is a finding.
- A figure of speech in the text's own register, or the writer's own voice in a signed text, first person included. A figure is an overclaim only where a reader would take it as a factual claim the text does not support, and there the first *Avoid* item decides; an *everything*, a *nothing* or a *never* that overstates in the way the figure means to is read as the figure it is.
- A subheading that states what its section says, where the section's point is not a quotation's judgement, figure or concession. A subheading that sums up its section says what the section says as a whole; that is its work, not a repeat, and it may name the section's limit or its setting rather than its most favourable result. Where the section's point is a quotation's judgement, figure or concession, a subheading that states that point pre-spends the quotation and stays a finding.
- A heading that shares names or topic words with the sentence under it while saying something that sentence does not. A repeat is a finding by what it says again, not by the words it shares.

Where you would word a working heading differently but can name no loss, record nothing against it: a note that it could be better is not a finding, and it licenses no change.

A subheading over a quotation that names the subject, the occasion or the speaker and leaves the quotation its point is working too, and not a subject named with nothing said about it.
# The anti-slop catalogue

Prose that a language model produced, or that a human wrote after reading a great deal of it, fails in a small number of recognisable ways. This is the catalogue of those ways: what each one looks like on the page, why it costs the reader something, and the smallest change that removes it. It is a diagnostic document — a Skill reading it beside the base contract meets no target the contract does not already hold, and a Skill reading it alone has the patterns and their repairs and needs nothing else.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language, and do not look for the English words in it. A word, a phrase, a punctuation convention, or a construction that only exists in one language belongs to that language's own anti-slop guidance instead, where a Skill loads it beside this file.

## The test before a pattern is recorded

Each pattern below says what a phrase looks like, and looking like one is not being one. Make the repair in your head before you record anything: where the text then asserts more, less or something else than it did, or a distinction it drew is gone, the pattern is not present and nothing is recorded. A hedge that marks genuine doubt, a repetition that lands, a contrast the reader really would otherwise draw wrongly — each of them fails that test, and each is left exactly as it stands.

The test comes before the finding rather than after it. A pattern written down reaches whoever repairs it as a defect somebody found, and a guard that only makes the repair careful arrives too late to save the phrase.

Repair with the smallest change that removes a pattern the test admits. The writer's vocabulary, their bluntness, their humour, their admitted uncertainty, and their rhythm are what makes a text theirs; a pass that tidies all of it into even prose has replaced one machine voice with another. Leave a strong sentence alone even where it is unusual.

## The seven patterns

**False contrasts.** A negation used as a run-up to the actual claim: *This isn't a tool. It's a way of working.* *The question isn't whether, but when.* *It's not just faster — it's cheaper.* The rejected half was never in play, so the sentence spends the reader's attention establishing a position nobody held. State the second half on its own: *This changes how the team works.* A contrast stays where the text really is correcting something a reader would otherwise believe.

**Empty openings.** A first sentence that announces the subject, asserts that the subject matters, or clears the throat before the text starts: *In today's rapidly changing landscape…*, *Communication has never been more important.*, *Here's the thing.*, *What most people get wrong is…* Each could sit in front of any text at all, which is the test: an opening that would survive being moved to a different article is carrying no information. Cut it and open on the material — a fact, a scene, a tension, the question the text answers. The second paragraph is very often the real opening.

**Importance inflation.** Adjectives and formulas that assert weight the material has not shown: *a pivotal moment*, *stands as a testament to*, *a game-changer*, *underscores the significance of*, *plays a vital role in*. Also the trailing participial clause that pretends to interpret — *…, highlighting the team's commitment to quality* — which adds a judgement no fact in the sentence supports. Replace the assertion with what actually happened: *The launch is the company's first paid product.* A reader who is given the fact will decide it matters without being told to.

**Vague attribution.** A claim credited to nobody: *Studies show*, *experts agree*, *industry reports suggest*, *it is widely believed*, *many argue*. Nothing here can be checked, and nothing can be contradicted, which is precisely what makes it comfortable to write. Name who found it, who said it, and how they know; where the text has no source, cut the claim rather than dressing it. Do not invent an attribution to satisfy the pattern — an unsourced sentence is removed, never furnished with a plausible source.

**Synonym cycling.** One thing given a new name every time it is mentioned, because repeating a word felt like poor style: *the agent* reviews the draft, then *the assistant* scores it, then *the tool* suggests fixes. A reader who has been introduced to three names reasonably assumes three things. Pick the clear name and repeat it. Repetition of a key term is how a reader knows it is the same term, and the fix is usually one word restored in two places rather than a rewritten paragraph. The pattern is present only where the names denote one thing: two words a text uses for two things are not cycling however often they alternate, and a text that named two things comes back naming two things.

**Robotic rhythm.** Sentences and paragraphs built to one template: the same length, the same shape, the same three-part list, each paragraph opening with its topic sentence and closing with its summary. Stacked short fragments used for drama — *That's it. That's the whole idea.* — are the same fault at the other extreme. Read a passage aloud in your head; where the breath falls in the same place every time, the shape is doing the writing. Vary length and construction where the meaning gives you a reason to, and merge or split only the sentences whose shape is actually the problem.

**Generic conclusions.** A final paragraph that restates what the reader has just read, reopens the introduction as a rhetorical question, or reaches for an uplifting abstraction: *In conclusion*, *Ultimately, the future belongs to those who…*, *one thing is clear.* The reader was there for the whole text and does not need it summarised back. Delete the paragraph and end on the last concrete point the draft already contains; where the job genuinely calls for a conclusion, a recommendation, or a next step, write that thing plainly and stop. Do not replace a weak closing metaphor with a better one — remove it.

      "source": "sv",
      "content": "Swedish is a V2 language: the finite verb is the second constituent of a main clause, so fronting anything at all pushes the subject behind the verb. Write *I morgon åker vi till Malmö*, never *I morgon vi åker till Malmö*. This is the single most common structural tell of a text drafted in English and rendered into Swedish.

Compounds are written as one word. *Kvalitetssäkring*, *kundtjänstmedarbetare*, *miljökonsekvensbeskrivning*. Splitting them is not a stylistic choice in Swedish and often changes the meaning outright — *en rökfri miljö* and *en rök fri miljö* are different claims. Where a compound grows unreadably long, rewrite it into a prepositional phrase rather than splitting it.

Definiteness is marked twice. An adjective before a definite noun takes both the front article and the noun's suffix: *den nya rapporten*, *det stora huset*, *de svenska kunderna*. English has one article and drafts translated from it routinely lose one of the two Swedish markers.

The s-passive is the ordinary Swedish passive and is shorter than its periphrastic alternative: *rapporten skickas på fredag*, not *rapporten blir skickad på fredag*. Both exist; the s-form is the unmarked one, and the *bli*-form carries a change-of-state reading that is often not intended.

*Du* is the default address in Swedish prose, including business and journalism. *Ni* to a single reader is either archaic or a deliberate distancing, and reads as a translation from a language that has a formal pronoun.

*Man* is a fallback rather than the ordinary generic pronoun. It is justified where the agent genuinely is anybody at all or is genuinely unknown, and where naming one would claim more than the material carries. Where the sentence has a real subject to hand — the reader, the writer, the organisation, the profession, the study — that subject is what the sentence takes. A text that reaches for *man* with any of those available reads as evasive, and it is usually where an English draft's *you*, *we*, or passive has landed rather than anything the writer chose.

Speech that the text reports is ordinarily set with a speech dash rather than in quotation marks: an interview answer, a remark at a meeting, anything a person said that the text renders readable. A writer reaches for quotation marks where the phrasing itself is the point — where it is what is new, where it is disputed, or where the text is about how the thing was said. What each of the two marks promises a reader, and what that makes each of them a claim about, is settled in Mechanics; this scope says only which one an ordinary Swedish text reaches for first.

Genitive takes a bare *s* with no apostrophe: *Kntnts kunder*, *Sveriges riksdag*. A name already ending in *s*, *x*, or *z* takes nothing at all: *Anders bok*, *Marx teori*.

Swedish tolerates a shorter sentence than English does and punishes subordination harder. Prefer a main clause with a fronted adverbial to a long relative construction, and prefer a verb to a nominalisation: *när kommunen beslutade* over *vid kommunens beslutsfattande*.

Reach for the established Swedish term where one exists and the field actually uses it — *återkoppling*, *underlag*, *avstämning* — but do not purge the loanwords a professional reader expects. A text that writes *dator* and *webbplats* naturally is Swedish; a text that hunts down every English term and replaces it with a coinage nobody says is not."
    },
    "review": {
      "source": "sv",
      "content": "Read for särskrivning first. A split compound is the error a Swedish reader notices before anything else, and generated or dictated text produces them in bulk.

Check the word order of every clause that opens with something other than the subject. A fronted adverbial, object, or subordinate clause must be followed immediately by the finite verb.

Nominal style is the characteristic failure of Swedish institutional prose. *Genomförande av en utvärdering av verksamheten* is three nouns doing the work of one verb; *utvärdera verksamheten* says it. Look for *-ande*, *-ning*, and *-else* nouns paired with a colourless verb — *ske*, *utföra*, *genomföra*, *möjliggöra* — and give the sentence its real verb back.

Watch the heavy pre-modifier: *den av kommunen beslutade planen*, *de i rapporten redovisade siffrorna*. It is grammatical and it is bureaucratic. Unpack it into a relative clause: *planen som kommunen beslutade om*.

Prepositional filler multiplies in Swedish official prose: *i syfte att* for *för att*, *avseende* and *gällande* for *om*, *utifrån* for *enligt* or *efter*, *i samband med* for *när*. Each costs words and none adds meaning.

Check that the register is one register. Swedish shifts sharply between *ni*-formality, *du*-directness, and youth-informal, and a text that mixes them reads as assembled rather than written.

Check reported speech for text-internal inconsistency in its quotation form. Fluent wording alone does not show that a quotation was repaired; without the source, leave that provenance claim unjudged. A change of mark may distinguish exact wording from rendered speech, so diagnose it only where the text gives grounds for a conflicting reading.

Read for the loan that arrived with the draft rather than with the field. *Regulatorer* is *tillsynsmyndigheter* or *myndigheter*, *adressera* in the sense of taking something up is *ta upp* or *behandla*, *leverera* in the sense of giving is *ge* or *erbjuda*, *metrik* is *mätvärde* or *nyckeltal*, and an *approach* is an *angreppssätt* or an *ansats*. The pairs are illustrative rather than a list to work through: which loans a Swedish text keeps is settled in Composition, and what a review adds is noticing the ones that are there because the sentence was thought in English.

Look for the English participle rendered mechanically as an *-ande* form. *Ökande kostnader* is Swedish; a paragraph in which every subject carries an *-ande* modifier is an English draft in Swedish clothes.

Finally, check the sentence rhythm the way a Swedish reader hears it: known information before new, one main idea per sentence, and no clause postponed behind three others."
    },
    "anti-slop": {
      "source": "sv",
      "content": "Openings that mark generated Swedish: *I dagens snabbrörliga värld*, *I en tid då*, *I en värld där*, *Det är viktigt att notera att*, *Låt oss dyka ner i*, *Låt oss titta närmare på*. Cut them; the sentence after them is the real opening.

Closings of the same kind: *Sammanfattningsvis*, *Avslutningsvis kan vi konstatera att*, *I slutändan handlar det om*, *Framtiden får utvisa*. A Swedish text that has made its point stops.

The imported false contrast: *Det handlar inte bara om X – det handlar om Y*, *Inte bara ... utan också ...*, *Det är inte X. Det är Y.* as a paragraph of its own. The construction exists in Swedish, but its density in generated text is the tell.

Metaphor stock: *en resa*, *navigera i landskapet*, *nyckeln till framgång*, *hörnstenen i*, *ta det till nästa nivå*, *game changer*, *att verkligen förstå kraften i*. These arrive as a set rather than because the writer meant any of them.

Superlative inflation: *revolutionerande*, *banbrytande*, *otroligt kraftfull*, *helt avgörande*, *oöverträffad*. Swedish general-interest prose is understated, and a text that reaches for these in every paragraph reads as advertising copy whatever it was meant to be.

Connective adverbs at the head of every paragraph — *Dessutom*, *Vidare*, *Följaktligen*, *Därtill*, *Sammantaget* — are a generation tell when they become a template for the text's progression.

A concentration of the objective punctuation errors identified in Mechanics is also evidence of English punctuation carried into generated Swedish. Refer to that scope for the forms; this scope does not restate them.

The triad reflex: *snabbt, enkelt och säkert*, *tydligt, tryggt och tillgängligt*. Three adjectives where the writer had one thing to say.

Empty attribution: *studier visar*, *experter menar*, *det är allmänt känt att*, with nobody named. In Swedish as in any language, an unattributed authority is a claim the writer has not made."

# Tallmora Energi inviger den 3 juni en ny solpark vid Kvarnbacken

Den 3 juni 2027 invigs Tallmora Energi AB:s nya solpark vid Kvarnbacken i Tallmora, på den mark där kommunens grustäkt låg fram till 2019. Parken har 12 000 solpaneler på 18 hektar, har kostat 64 miljoner kronor att bygga och beräknas ge 7,5 gigawattimmar el om året.

”Solparken visar att en gammal grustäkt kan göra nytta igen. Vi tror att fler kommuner kommer att pröva samma lösning”, säger Maria Ekholm, vd för Tallmora Energi.

Årsproduktionen på 7,5 gigawattimmar motsvarar enligt bolagets egen beräkning hushållselen i omkring 1 500 villor i kommunen. Siffran för årsproduktionen är en uppskattning, och den verkliga produktionen beror på hur soligt året blir. Elen levereras till elnätet och säljs inte direkt till hushållen i närheten.

Området är inhägnat och inte öppet för allmänheten, utom vid invigningen den 3 juni klockan 14.00–16.00, då bolaget visar parken för besökare.

”Vi vill att elen som används i Tallmora också ska produceras här”, säger Johan Berg, styrelseordförande i Tallmora Energi.

Grustäkten vid Kvarnbacken avvecklades 2019. Tallmora Energi fick tillstånd att bygga solparken 2025, och bygget började i augusti 2026.

Parken har 40 växelriktare. Panelerna står i rader i öst–västlig riktning, och markytan mellan raderna betas av får från en gård i närheten.

Bilder från solparken finns på https://example.se/press/kvarnbacken-bilder.

Kontakt: Lina Sjögren, kommunikationschef, Tallmora Energi, 070-000 00 00, lina.sjogren@example.se

Tallmora Energi AB ägs av Tallmora kommun och levererar el och fjärrvärme till omkring 14 000 kunder i kommunen.
EOF
